sections.title: Collecting & Preserving Arthropods, at a Glance
Collecting & Preserving Arthropods, at a Glance

blocks.x: Medical entomology depends on getting real specimens out of the field and into the lab intact and identifiable. This module walks through insect biology and life cycles, why and how entomological surveys are planned, the equipment and seven core sampling methods used across insect groups, group-specific techniques for winged and wingless adults and ticks, and finally how specimens are killed, preserved, and pinned for study.

Insects are the most diverse group of life on Earth, making up more than two-thirds of all known organisms. Nearly all undergo either complete (holometabolous) or incomplete (hemimetabolous) metamorphosis, a distinction that shapes how each life stage must be sampled.
The CDC recognises three purposes for entomological surveys: exploratory surveys to determine the fauna of an area, surveys to appraise control operations, and epidemiological studies.
Hand picking, collecting nets (aerial and aquatic), aspirators, sifters (Berlese funnels), light traps, baited traps, and combing — each suited to a different arthropod group, life stage, or habitat.

Specimens are killed with agents such as chloroform or ethyl acetate, preserved in fluids like 70–80% ethyl alcohol, and larger insects are pinned, wrapped, boxed, and carefully labelled with genus and species.
Before collecting a single specimen, it helps to understand what insects are and how their bodies change across a life cycle — because the collecting method has to match the life stage.

blocks.x: 01Insects: The Most Diverse Life on Earth

items: Insects are the most diverse and abundant forms of life on Earth — more than 2/3 of all known organisms.
Insects undergo either complete or incomplete metamorphosis (egg → larva → pupa → adult insect).
Larva have a soft tubular body and look like worms.
Larvae of flying insects are called "maggots."

To determine the fauna of an area.

Insect surveys conducted as part of epidemiological investigations.

items: Simple and sometimes effective with large terrestrial insects, such as cockroaches, where they are picked by hand and put into a bottle (usually with perforated lids or nets to permit free air circulation).
Useful for several ectoparasites that can be directly picked from the skin of infected persons, like fleas, mites, and lice.
Tools often used alongside this method include forceps, for very small specimens or vectors of concern.
An effective device for collecting small crawling insects that can be found on surfaces as free-living organisms.
It operates by a simple mouth suction technique.
Uses a kind of sifter, or a Berlese funnel, to collect insects that live in ground litter, rotting wood, fungi, or shore debris.
The size of the mesh depends on the size of the specimens sought.

To use the sifter: place the material to be sifted into the container and shake it gently over a white pan or piece of white fabric. As insects and mites fall onto the fabric, they may be collected with forceps, a brush, or an aspirator.

items: With light traps, advantage is taken of the attraction of many insects to a light source, which increases in activity at night.

The mosquito light trap employs an electric light bulb as an attractant and an electric fan to create a current of air, which forces the mosquitoes through a wire net cone into a killing jar. This is a useful device for collecting many species.
A disadvantage is that the light source is also attractive to many other insects, so the mosquitoes must be sorted from a hodgepodge of moths, beetles, and bugs.
Flies may be captured by traps baited with materials attractive as food or as egg-laying sites.
Effective for houseflies and several species of fleshflies and blowflies.
Mixed baits containing substances attractive to various species can be used.
The traps are usually exposed for 24 hours.
Bait-trap catches are used chiefly to obtain qualitative information on the occurrence of various species and on broad differences in the composition of fly populations.
Some vectors that live on furred animals or livestock can be obtained for study by combing them from the animal.
Care is taken to avoid spreading parasites to other animals.
Gloves and protective clothing are advised for the collector.
Repellents may be used to detach some insects before combing, to ensure their release from the skin of the host.
Terrestrial larvae are usually collected using forceps into containers with perforated lids for study, e.g. fly maggots.
Aquatic larvae are sampled using transparent plastic or glass containers, with the water they exist in, e.g. mosquito larvae.
With insects that undergo incomplete metamorphosis, the nymphs are collected similarly to the adult stages, since they share the same basic morphology.

blocks.x: For mosquitoes, sandflies, tsetse flies, and blackflies:

items: Light traps — attract and catch mosquitoes drawn to light, e.g. Culex species.
Gravid traps — a water-filled container with an attractant lures female mosquitoes ready to lay eggs.
Backpack aspirators — a motorized fan and collection net vacuum up mosquitoes from vegetation or walls.
CDC miniature light traps — smaller, battery-operated versions of light traps, easy to transport for field studies.
Resting boxes — dark, sheltered boxes or tubes placed where mosquitoes are known to rest.
Human landing catches — a person allows mosquitoes to land on them before capture; controversial due to disease-transmission risk, and not widely used.

blocks.x: Sampling methods for wingless ectoparasites such as fleas and ticks include:

items: Direct visual inspection
Manual combing
Shaking of potential host animals
Flotation of faecal samples
Aspirators or light traps

blocks.x: The most common methods used for sampling ticks include:

items: Drag samplers, using clothes
Flannel mater samplers
Tick tubes, glass tubes
Blanket drag sampling, using a woollen blanket
Flagging and sweeping
Pyrethrum aerosol spray sampling

blocks.x: Once collected, specimens must be humanely killed and preserved in a way that keeps their diagnostic features intact for later identification.

items: Chloroform
Ether
Ethyl acetate
Ethylene tetrachloride
Carbon tetrachloride
UV lights
70–80% ethyl alcohol
3% glycerol
7–10% formalin
Alternatives: undiluted alcoholic drinks (whisky, brandy, or gin), petrol, or kerosene
Avoid preserving specimens under direct sunlight, to prevent heat damage
For some insects, like horseflies and tsetse flies, soft toilet paper or cotton wool is used for wrapping them after pinning.
Keep and transport pinned specimens in a cardboard box.
Label appropriately with the genus and species of the specimen.
